title_en: Vaishnav Gopaldas Is Accepted as the True Guru
translation:
On the eighth day of the bright half of Shravan in Samvat 1660, the Vaishnav Jivandasji manifested at the age of eleven in Gahej Goriyad. There the true dharma revealed itself to him. But he always cherished the wish that wherever a Vaishnav was to be found, he might have the good fortune of asking about sakhi (devotional couplets) and see love for God deepen. When he turned sixteen, at Keslubaa (present-day Kesaru, near Palej) he had his very first meeting with Gopaldasji, the Barot (bard-poet) of Chorenda. Jivandasji greeted Gopaldasji with "Ram Ram." Gopaldasji was returning from another village where he had performed someone's last rites. Jivandasji then invited Gopaldasji to his own temple-home, brought him there, and they sang hari-kirtan (devotional hymns); on that occasion satsang and holy company continued for a full day and night. From there Gopaldasji returned to his own temple-abode.

In Samvat 1683, on the thirteenth day of the dark half of Aso, Jivandasji went to Chorenda. There satsang and holy company happened again, and a very long discussion took place on whether God has form or is formless. Citing evidence from the nitya-akshari (word-for-word) exposition of Namdev, Kabirji, Adhyaruji, the Bhagavad Gita, the Bhagavat, the Shiv Mahimna Stotra, Hariram Vyas (disciple of Hit Harivansh), Rankavanka, Govinddas's Sarvang Leela, the verses of Jaydevji's Geet Govind, the words of Vidurji in the Mahabharat, the sayings of Premanand, the sayings of Jaswantji, and the couplets in the sahasranama (thousand-name hymns) of Seni, Dhana, Peepa, Rohidas, Mirabai, Surdas and others, they arrived at a conclusion on whether God is sagun-sakar (with attributes and form) or nirgun-nirakar (without attributes, formless). The final conclusion reached was this: the true Supreme Being is the enchanting Flute-Player (Moral Manohar) sung of in the Vedas, spoken of in the Bhagavad Gita, described in the Bhagavat and in the sahasranama — He is the true Lord of Namdev and Kabirji. This entire universe has lost its way on this point. Just as the Lord of the clouds is the ocean, and the Kshirsagar's waves are His waves, so too the divine plays (leela) and incarnations — Ram, Krishna, and the rest — are like the waves of that same ocean; among all these incarnations, Ram and Krishna are the principal ones bearing His name and form. All the other incarnations, however, are merely the names given to the forms that God assumed. Those incarnations, therefore, were like the sixteen ornaments (adornments) worn by the sakhis (companions) of the Rasa circle — in their adornment one could see only Krishna's reflection, not the original Krishna. The original Krishna was the one on whose shoulder Radhaji placed her hand while dancing the Rasa — He alone was the true Krishna. Thus these incarnations were like waves of the ocean; they were but one form of that original God. So the conclusion reached was this: the true Supreme Being is the enchanting Flute-Player who resided in Radha's hand — the one bearing the Name upon whom the form rested. As for the rest — the various forms of the incarnations that bore that form's name — they are but one glimpse (a partial reflection) of God, and cannot be counted as the complete Parabrahm (Supreme Absolute). Thus the Deity who is Name-and-then-Form is the true one, but the deity who is Form-and-then-Name is not the complete Supreme Being. Having resolved every doubt about God's form and formlessness in this way, Jivandasji Maharaj accepted Sadguru Gopaldasji as his own true Guru — this took place when he went to Chorenda on the thirteenth day of the bright half of Aso in Samvat 1683, on the day of the Sharad Purnima festival. _Paani peena chhaanke, guru karna jaanke_ (Water should be drunk only after straining it, and a guru should be made only after knowing him well) — meaning that just as water must be filtered before drinking, one must be certain of a guru's worthiness before accepting him. It was on this occasion that Jivanji Maharaj spoke these words:

_Kaamika guru kaamini, lobhika guru daam._
_Kabirka guru bhagat hai, bhagatanke guru Ram._
_Guru kije vicharke, jehi bataave Ram._
_Sarju teere Jeevana, nagar Ayodhya gaam._
(The lustful man's guru is the woman he desires; the greedy man's guru is money. Kabir's guru is the true devotee, and the devotee's guru is Ram Himself. Choose a guru only after due thought — one who can truly reveal Ram to you. — Thus speaks Jivan[a], on the banks of the Sarayu, in the town of Ayodhya, [of the Ram who dwells there].)

Men driven by lust fall into the snare of women; being under the sway of a woman or wife, they must live as she dictates. A greedy man, on the other hand, holds money dear, and so falls into the trap of whoever dangles wealth before him. But a truly worthy guru is one like Kabir — a real saint, for true saints are devoted only to the worship of Ram. Hence it is said: before making anyone one's guru, one must think carefully whether he can give true conviction of Ram — the guru chosen should be one who can grant true realization of Ram of Ayodhya, of what He truly is. Jivandasji, in his quest for truth, resolved to make a saint his guru, but the question was how to recognize a true saint. Renunciants and ascetics can be found in plenty, but how does one know a true saint, and by what test can he be recognized? So he planted a dry, dead stump of a banyan tree in his courtyard, resolving that he would accept as his guru whichever saint's charanamrit (water that has washed a saint's feet) made that dry stump turn green. Saints passing on their pilgrimage-circuit (parikrama) of the river Reva-Narmada were served by him; he would wash their feet and water the dead stump with that charanamrit. As word of this vow (tek) spread, people began to think Jivandasji had gone mad. Some said that no saint should be tested in such a manner, and that this had corrupted the intellect of these Brahmins. Yet an inner voice assured him that a saint like Kabir would indeed be found this way. Jivanji Maharaj wandered and struggled a great deal; he had even, for a time, taken sannyasis (renunciate ascetics) as his guru. But finally, to secure a true guru, he tested Gopaldasji thoroughly and, once he had understood the real truth, accepted him as his guru. From childhood he had wandered and struggled; the true dharma had revealed itself to him from the age of eleven, and by the time he reached maturity he had also grown wise. It was for this reason that he made such an untiring, deep effort to be certain of Gopaldasji's worthiness. And Gopaldasji proved that his own view and path were indeed the ones that lead to true bhakti (devotion).
